spans.text: Saturday, mid-January. Halsey Wealth Partners, 14th floor, Back Bay. Adam Halsey's corner office. Late afternoon, the kind where the building heat is already off for the weekend.

The floor was empty the way a trading floor is never empty on a weekday and always empty on a Saturday in January. The cleaners came Sunday nights. The heat ran on a weekday schedule and had clicked off at one. By four the windows had started to give the cold back into the room, and the radiators along the base of the glass ticked as they cooled, the only sound on the floor besides the elevator, which had run once in the last hour, and the carpet under a single pair of shoes coming down the long side of the building toward the corner.

Adam Halsey sat at his desk with his coat on the back of the door and a folder squared in front of him. He had squared it three times. The light at the window was the four o'clock light, which in January was already the wrong color, a flat gray that took the warmth out of the wood and made the room look like a photograph of the room. On the credenza behind him there was a framed photograph of the first office, two rooms over a bank on Federal Street, and the firm's first brass plate, which had hung by the door of those two rooms and now sat propped against a book where he could see it from the chair.

He had come in at two. The guard in the lobby on a Saturday was a young one, weekend man, and he had signed Adam in on the clipboard and said cold one, Mr. Halsey, and Adam had said cold one, and the young guard had not known him, which was new, there had been forty years of guards in that lobby who knew him and now there was a young one on a Saturday who checked the name on the clipboard against the badge, and Adam had let him check it, and had ridden up alone.

He had walked the floor before he sat down. He did that now on the Saturdays, walked the dark floor first, and he walked it to the names on the doors and said them in the dark in the order of the doors. Vega. The empty bracket. Crowe. He walked to the corner where the foundation stair went down and stood at the top of it a moment and did not go down. He came back along the windows. He stopped at the conference room glass and looked at the chairs the cleaners had pushed in at their one angle and he said the quarter's numbers to himself, the firm-wide return, the number of families, the dollars under management, four point two billion, fourteen families, and he had them, all of them, clean, and he stood at the glass with the numbers clean in him the way a man stands on a dock and puts his weight on a plank before he trusts it with the day.

Then he had gone into his office and taken out the folder and made it thin, on purpose, because the thinness was the message, and he had squared it, and squared it again, and he had taken the brass plate down off the wall by the door where it had hung for fourteen years in this office as it had hung for two years over the bank, and he had set it on the credenza against the book, propped, the year facing the chair, eighty-five, where he could see it while he talked to her, and he could not have said to the young guard or to anyone why he wanted the year where he could see it, only that he had wanted it there, and had put it there, and had sat down to wait for the one person he had asked to come in on a Saturday in the cold.
Iris stood in the doorway with her coat still on.
You came in on a Saturday for this,
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: You said it was the annual review.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: I said it was the annual review.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: She set her coat over the back of the chair and sat down. He pushed a single folder across the desk. It was thin. The annual reviews were never thin. The annual reviews ran to forty pages and came in a binder with tabs and took two hours, and he ran them himself, and he had never once in nine years moved one to a Saturday.
How long have you been my chief of staff.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: And before that, two years as my analyst.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: One year. The year before that I was at McKinsey.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: He turned his chair toward the window. Across the avenue the office towers had their weekend lights on, every third floor, the pattern a building makes when no one has chosen it and a timer has. He looked at the pattern. The radiator ticked.
I started this firm in eighty-five,
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: Two rooms over a bank. You couldn't get a desk up the stairs. We took the legs off.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: You started the firm in eighty-seven. The plate says eighty-five, but the plate's two years young.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: He looked at the plate against the book on the credenza. He looked at it the way a man looks at a clock he does not trust.
The plate says eighty-five. You came to the fish men in eighty-seven.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: I took the legs off the desk in eighty-five.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: You took the legs off the desk before you ever came to them. The desk was always the desk.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: She did not say anything else about it. She did not say it the way you correct a person. She said it the way you hand a person a thing they have dropped, without making them watch you bend down.
I'm going to choose a successor by July. I'm telling three people that I'm looking at them. You're one of them. Marcus is one of them. Sophie is one of them.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: She did not move. The coat she had set over the chair slid an inch and she did not reach for it.
You're not going to ask me anything,
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: I'm going to. I'm getting there.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: There's no board. There are four partners and an outside compliance attorney.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: She put her hand flat on the folder. She did not open it. The folder was the kind the firm used for client work, heavy stock, the corner embossed, and her hand covered the embossing.

I want a five-year client retention plan for the Beaumont family. Not the firm. The Beaumont family. I want the names of the people inside that family who are going to want to leave us in years two and four. I want what we say to them. I want what we do if they go anyway.

Because they're a billion one. Because Henry is going to push for a change. Because if we lose them we lose two other families inside eighteen months. Because the next person in this chair has to know the inside of that family the way I know it.
Or be capable of learning it.
Or be capable of learning it.
You tell me. That's the homework.
I'll tell you now and you tell me if I'm wrong.

Henry wants out. Henry has wanted out since the trust restructured in nineteen. He thinks we cost too much and do too little and he's half right, which is the dangerous half. Cyrus will never leave while he's alive. So the question isn't Cyrus. The question is the grandchildren.
The two daughters. Caroline and the younger one.

Pilar. Caroline will follow Henry because Caroline does what Henry does. Pilar won't follow anyone, which is why Pilar is the one we lose in year four, after Cyrus, when there's no one left in that family who remembers why they hired us.
Because in eighty-seven Cyrus's brother put the whole family into a thing that went to zero and we were the ones who said don't.
He looked at the plate on the credenza again and then back at her.

Year two we keep Caroline by keeping Henry from feeling small. Year four we keep Pilar by giving her a reason that isn't her grandfather. If you can't write the year-four page, write me a page that says you can't write it yet and why.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: He turned the chair back. The motion was a half second slow at the end, the chair coasting the last few degrees, and he stopped it with his foot. He pulled the folder back across the desk toward himself and opened it and closed it again without reading it.
The legacy book. Old, Driscoll, the two Pearson trusts, Mrs. Tan, and the Okonkwo family. Six clients. The smallest book in the firm.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: The next person is going to want to do something about the legacy book.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: What is there to do about it.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: Nothing. That's the answer. The next person is going to look at six clients who take more hours than the Beaumonts and decide they're a rounding error, and they're going to be wrong, and I want to know which of the three of you is wrong about it.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: You want me to put the legacy book in the Beaumont plan.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: I want you to leave the legacy book out of the Beaumont plan and tell me you left it out on purpose.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: I'm not writing anything down. I don't have the folder open.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: He looked at her hand on the desk and then at the closed folder under his own hand.
He turned the chair a few degrees back toward the window and then back to her, and he was looking at her the way he looked at her when he was about to ask her something he had already decided.
I want you to know that I'm not telling you to do this because you're the one. I'm telling you to do this because I want to see what you do.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: He nodded once. He looked at the folder.
I think I need a coffee,
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: There's no one here on a Saturday. I'll make it.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: There's no one here on a Saturday because I told them not to come in.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: She stood up. She picked up her coat from where it had slid and put it over her arm and did not put it on.
You said two years as your analyst.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: I'm telling you because someone is going to ask you that question in a meeting and you're going to answer two.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: She went out along the corridor toward the kitchen at the center of the floor, past the dark offices, past the glass-walled conference room where the chairs were pushed in at exactly the same angle because the cleaners pushed them in and no one had sat in them since. The brass nameplates by the office doors caught what light there was, Vega, Crowe, an empty bracket where a name had been taken down and not replaced. The kitchen had the smell a kitchen has when the machine has been off all day, the rinsed-out smell of a sink and a drain and the faint sweet of the milk in the door of the refrigerator. She ran the machine. It coughed and primed and she stood with her arm folded across her and her coat over the other arm and watched the cup fill, and the sound of the machine was the loudest thing on the floor.

She made it the way he took it. Cream and one. She carried it back along the corridor. The light through the conference room glass had gone the color the windows go when the lights are off inside and the city is on outside.

When she came back he was looking at the same place on the desk where the folder had been. The folder was in her hand. She had picked it up off the corner of the desk without noticing she had done it.

He took it. He did not drink it. He set it on the leather coaster that lived on the right side of the desk and turned the cup so the handle pointed the way it always pointed, and he did all of that the way a man does a thing his hands know, and then he left the cup alone.
How long have you been my chief of staff.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: He looked at the cup he had not drunk. He looked at the window. The pattern across the avenue had not changed.
At the start. When you came in.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: I'm saying so now. You said it now.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: He turned the chair a quarter turn and back.
That's the homework I'm not going to write down,
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: I'll tell you who you are, Iris, and you don't have to do a plan for it. You're the one who lets a man find the door himself and stands close enough to catch him if he doesn't.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: That's not in the folder either.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: Don't open the folder until Monday.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: And don't tell Naomi if she calls you.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: I know she has your number.
spans.speaker: Adam

spans.text: She put her coat on. She set the folder back down on the corner of the desk where he could see it, square to the edge, and she squared it once with two fingers. She did not say goodbye. She did not say have a good weekend. She walked out and the door did not click closed behind her because the door never clicked closed when you were the one closing it. The latch had been a quarter inch out of true for fourteen years, and Adam had been complaining about it for fourteen years, and three building engineers had looked at it and one had filed a work order and the work order had outlived the engineer.

At the elevator she pressed the button and the car was where she had left it, fourteen, the doors already open, the cab light too bright after the dark floor. She held the door with her hand and looked back down the corridor at the one lit office in the corner. She let the door go.

He sat with the coffee for ten minutes. He didn't drink it. The room cooled. The radiator stopped ticking, which meant it had gone all the way cold. Across the avenue the third-floor lights held their pattern and a window on the nineteenth floor of the building opposite went dark, someone else who had come in on a Saturday and was now going home.

When he stood up the folder was no longer where she had left it. He had moved it. It was square to the edge on the left side of the blotter now, under his hand, and he stood with his hand on it and looked at it. He didn't remember moving it. He looked at the corner of the desk where she had set it, and then at his hand, and he stood like that for a while.

On the credenza the brass plate caught the city light. Eighty-five. He picked it up and turned it over. The back was bare. He had never looked at the back. He set it down against the book the way it had been, the year facing out, and he turned it a half inch so it sat square the way the folder sat square, and he stood over it a moment longer.
He picked up the cold coffee and carried it to the kitchen himself and poured it out and rinsed the cup and set it in the rack, and the running water was the loudest thing on the floor.

He got his coat off the back of the door. He turned off the light. In the dark the city came up brighter in the glass. He stood in the doorway of his own office the way Iris had stood in it an hour before, with his coat on, and he looked at the desk, and the folder was a pale square in the dark, and he could not from the doorway have said whether it was on the left or the corner, and he did not go back in to check. He pulled the door. It did not click.
Saturday, early evening. Storrow Drive, westbound. Iris's car. The river on the right gone dark, the lights of Cambridge on the far bank. The phone face up on the passenger seat.

The phone lit before it rang, the way it does, the name up on the seat in the dark of the car for half a second before the sound. Naomi. Iris let it ring twice. She turned the radio off, which was already off. She picked it up at the third ring and put it to her ear and kept both hands near the wheel.
The river was on her right. A runner went by under a lamp and was gone.
I don't know Adam's Saturday, Naomi. I know mine.

There was a sound on the line that was a kitchen sound, a cabinet, water. Naomi was home. Naomi was making something or cleaning something while she did this, which was a thing Naomi did, which was the thing she did when the call was the thing and the cabinet was the cover.
You'd know if he moved it. You keep the calendar.
The Pike was coming up. Iris stayed left.
If Adam moved a meeting, the person to ask is Adam.
spans.speaker: Iris

spans.text: I'm not asking you what's on the calendar, Iris. I've been married to him for thirty-one years. I'm asking you how he was.
Naomi did not say anything for a moment. The water shut off on her end.
I've always said it. He says it too. He says it like it's the highest thing a person can be.
spans.speaker: Naomi

spans.text: It's not the highest thing a person can be.
No. It's not. But it's the thing he needs, so it's the thing he praises.

I'm not trying to pick the lock. I want you to know that. I called because I wanted to hear your voice and find out from your voice the thing you're not going to say. And I've found it out. So I'm going to let you drive.

I know you didn't. That's how I found it out. You answer every question I've ever asked you. You answered two of mine tonight and you didn't answer the third one, and you've never once not answered the third one.
Drive safe. Call me if you ever want to. You won't. Drive safe.

Iris put the phone back on the seat, face down this time. She drove. The lights of the far bank slid along the water. At the split she went left toward home and the river fell away behind the wall, and she drove the rest of it with both hands on the wheel and the radio off, and at a long light on the other side she picked the phone up and looked at it and the screen was dark and she put it back down without doing anything to it.
